review:
PEAK was a peak experience indeed. 

When I first started, I hopped into the official Discord to find a group. Most runs were hit or miss, but eventually I teamed up with this guy named 'Dex.' We managed to get our first win together, and since it was a first win for both of us, we knew we had to keep going.

We pushed through until around Ascent 3 or 4 before calling it a night. Little did I know, Dex would become a regular. Over the next week, we grinded the badges and ascents, spending nearly 30 hours together, and finally beat Ascent 7. 

This dude stuck with me all the way like a mad lad.

Dex, if you see this, you're a real one.

10/10 would random queue again.

Now i really don't have time to play a lot of games because of my job and that makes me sad, i wish i could experience more with this game and play it with my friends. Maybe i'll do it in the future but for now i enjoyed it for what it was.

I once nearly fell off a tall mountain during a trip, and my friend pulled me back at the very last second. Ever since that day, seeing a hand reaching out from above fills me with a strange mix of trust, fear, and adrenaline. Maybe he has forgotten about it by now, but for me it was a moment where I truly believed my life was ending. I’m still grateful he was there, and I’ll never forget what he did for me.

PEAK brought that feeling back. It captures the fear of slipping, the comfort of teamwork, and that rare moment when you know someone is there for you. A simple idea delivered with beautiful clarity.
I shot our worst team player with a blow dart, stuck him to a cactus, and then ate him. This game is an unwritten novel with every run. 10/10 would climb again.

This game is clearly meant to be played with friends… and I don’t really have anyone to play it with 🫶
Still, playing it solo felt way more meaningful than I expected. The atmosphere, the silence, and that constant feeling of pushing forward really stay with you 🎮✨
It never felt empty, just personal. Even alone, it’s absolutely worth playing 💙

Having just summited my 100th Peak, now finally feels like the right time to leave a review for this incredible game. I bought this originally with the intent of just adding it to my friendslop pile for a few hours of silly co-op, but it only took a few runs for me to quickly realise how much care went into the design of this game. It's had me tearing my hair out in frustration, sweating, and heart pounding so many times (and I'm a big Souls fan so that's saying something). I've enjoyed co-op but I'd say about 80% of my peaks were solo and not a single moment was dull or felt lonely - the beautiful soundtrack and biome designs have you fully immersed throughout your journey. I've been playing since the original biome setup and have thoroughly enjoyed the additions and can't wait to see the teased biome that is yet to come. You'd think after 100 Peaks (and that's not counting my many failed attempts) this game would start to feel a bit stale but the new map seeds every 24hrs and biome rotations keep things feeling fresh and exciting and importantly, offer a new challenge each time giving unlimited replayability! As someone restricted to the house for most of my time due to immunosuppressants, I can honestly say that Peak has given me something fun and meaningful to look forward to and achieve each day after I log off remote work. On reflection, it's obscene that this game only cost me six quid - needless to say I've gotten more than my money's worth and I know I'll get many more hours out of this game :)

I don't think PEAK is just a game about climbing a mountain.

Somehow, it's become one of the nicest places I've ever spent time in.

Yes, you can play it with your friends. You can scream when someone falls, and laugh at a friend slipping on a banana. But somewhere between all of that, you start talking about your day, about life, about things you probably wouldn't have brought up if you were just sitting in a Discord call with nothing to do.

PEAK gives you something to do while you're spending time with the people you care about. And I think that's what makes it so special.

And somehow, it's just as lovely alone, when your friends aren't around, PEAK doesn't suddenly become an empty experience. There's something strangely peaceful about climbing by yourself. It's you, the mountain, and the quiet determination to see how far you can make it. The game is challenging, but it also has this warmth to it that I genuinely can't explain.

I've played plenty of games that are fun.

I've played games with better graphics, bigger worlds, and more things to do.

But I don't think I've ever experienced a game quite like PEAK. I genuinely think that's what makes this game so lovely. It's the feeling that, for a little while, you're exactly where you want to be.

I've never been able to experience a game quite like this before.

I know a [i]friendslop[/i] when I see one. A game subgenre where the lack of strong core mechanics and gameplay loops are replaced with incentives to get a reaction out of you with the cheapest possible tricks on the basis of your friends, not the game. 

This, is [b]not a friendslop. [/b]

This game took a lot of beating at first by being the headliner for the friendslop subgenre but the consistent fanbase proved otherwise. First of all, the game is extremely well made and well thought out. Everything feels intentional and none of them is frustrating, the gameplay loop is interesting, challenging, and full of variety and surprises. The world gen is really the cornerstone for this variety in gameplay and with each biome comes different challenges you must face. Other than that, its extremely rewarding and keeps you determined through all those challenges to reach the top to see the tail of that campfire smoke.

Other than that, the gameplay mechanics like the stamina bar getting replaced with various debuffs is very interesting and fun. I think that part of the survival gimmick is what makes the game so interesting in the first place, and the way that survival mechanic is neatly bound to everything that happens in the world around you is really complemental because it makes you feel more connected and inside the biome.

Obviously its way more fun with friends, obviously its way more unforgettable with friends. But that doesn't make it a friendslop. Not every coop game is friendslop and this game is a good anectode for all lazy friendslop developers out there trying to make a quick buck out of your 5 second reactions with simple gimmicks.

[h3][b]Friendslop[/b][/h3]
I know there's been lotta debate about the term "Friendslop" ever since co-op games like Lethal Company, Content Warning, R.E.P.O., PEAK, and you name it, started being labeled as Friendslop. Even older games before the term existed are somehow being considered "Friendslop".

I understand why lotta people who love these games feel disrespected by the term. The word "slop" already has a pretty negative connotation. We hear it in things like "AI-slop," where it usually describes something cheap, low-effort, or mass-produced.

I use the term because I see it as a "new genre" of co-op games, games designed around playing with more than 2 people. Just like how we use terms like "Metroidvania," "Souls-like", "Simulator", or "Incremental". They are genre that help us describe games that share certain characteristics. Not to mention I don't use "Friendslop" as an insult. I hope it finds a new term that fits better.

And you'll see comments like, [i]"You just hate it because you don't have friends or a group to play with"[/i] or, [i]"Your group probably gets bored with these games easily."[/i] But I don't think that's necessarily true.

Games like R.E.P.O. and MecCha Chameleon have public servers, so you aren't completely locked out of the experience just because your usual group isn't online. You can drop into a random lobby and play with strangers. Or you can find people through the community (discord, example). And maybe you might get along with them. And then add each other afterward, play again, or move on to another Friendslop game.

Now, let's say you already have a group to play with. Another comment pops up. [i]"You paid for a Friendslop game and only got an hour or so of fun. Is it "wasted" your time?"[/i] How about I ask you a familiar question, amigo.

1. What's the difference between that and going to the cinema, where you pay for a 2-3 hour movie?
2. What's the difference between that and going to a concert, where you might pay even more for a few hours of show?

Is it waste your time? i don't think so. I don't think the value determined by its duration. What makes something worth it can be the moment, the experience, or the memory.

When I think about the value of a game, I usually look at what the game itself gives me, "How much content it has, how many hours I can play, how many mechanics it has, or how much there is left to discover?"

Let me take examples from my 2 friendslop games, R.E.P.O. and PEAK. After hundreds of hours spent in both, I've noticed that they share a lot in common. But there's one major difference: [b][i]One has an endpoint, one does not.[/i][/b]

1. R.E.P.O.'s core is on moments with people. The gameplay itself is just the medium. No matter how many levels you clear, it just keeps going.  It runs on an endless loop. The levels get harder and harder until you eventually fail. "Winning" a round just unlocks... another round.

2. PEAK, has an actual endpoint, an achievable finish line, and that is reaching the peak. Once you're up there, the run is over and you did it. Because of that, its core leans more toward its gameplay mechanics. Stamina, hunger, health, weight, items, and even reading the routes through each biome all matter if you want to reach the peak. If you fail, you can restart, find another route, and plan a new strategy.

These two games have different focuses, but they still share a similar experience. And I'm glad that both managed to achieve such good longevity. Updates like cosmetics in R.E.P.O., or new biomes in PEAK. Also, the modding community that can completely change the way you experience these games, adding new mechanics, challenges, and making the game even more fun and chaotic.

I believe what Friendslop really about is not the "Slop". Sometimes, you just want to hang out with other people. And video games happen to be one of the places where we can do that. The game becomes a social space.

With friends, the game becomes a frame for shared memories.
With strangers, every lobby becomes a kind of social experiment. You don't know who you're going to meet. You play with them and maybe you'll never see them again. Or maybe you'll add each other afterward and end up playing together again later.

These games can even give you a reason to bring your old friend back from the grave. Someone you haven't talked to in months suddenly texted, [i]"Wanna play?"[/i] And for a few hours, you're just hanging out again.

[hr]
[i]Until eventually, the time ends. The updates get old. The server closes. And one day you stop playing entirely. Maybe your friends do too. But you still remember what happened. The dumb decisions. The accidental betrayals. The screaming. The unpredictable one. [b]The game was never the entire experience. The people are too. The game becomes a place where you make the memory.[/b][/i]

For newcomers, the concept of the game sounds incredibly simple:
Climb through different biomes, manage your wounds and hunger.

Sounds easy, right?

Well… achieving it with my bro took nearly 20 hours.
(I died, but hey, at least one of us made it out.)

Now sitting at around 40 hours with most of the achievements unlocked, I can safely say the real fun isn’t in collecting them.
It’s in the memories we made along the way.
The laughs, the happy moments… and even the times we were raging and arguing.
Because we didn’t give up. We kept trying, climbing again and again until we finally made it.

Each day, a new island is generated procedurally, ensuring no two runs are the same.
It constantly forces you to rethink your decisions, because even the tiniest mistake can ruin your run.

Sometimes the path that looks like the best one ends up being the worst, and the smartest thing you can do is turn back before it’s too late.
Or risking a climb that seems safe, only to slip and fall to your death... or barely survive, but with so little stamina left that the rest of the run becomes a struggle.
Or misusing an item because you had no idea what it actually does, only realizing your mistake when it actually mattered.

Would I board that plane again, crash onto an abandoned island, and try to reach the peak?
Absolutely.
And my bro is coming with me too. No arguments. Period.

Was waiting until the final update to make this review. PEAK is one of the most fun, creative, and unique indies to come out within the past couple of years. 

With a randomly generated map every 24 hours, and different luggage contents every new run, the game manages to make every new run feel unique but also not feel too reliant on RNG. Whether you're just BARELY scraping by or making the comeback of a generation, every run is different and interesting, and as long as you play smart and react effectively with the items you DO have, you WILL make it to the top of the mountain. It's a tough balance that the PEAK Devs NAILED.

Probably my favorite thing about PEAK is that even when you're failing, you're having FUN! You can have a really rough run, or make a dumb mistake that costs you the run, and you're still having a good time. Most of the time failure also feels earned and feels like YOU did something wrong, and you know how to react next time to avoid it in the future. And the rare times a death wasn't necessarily your fault, usually it's something so ridiculous you can't help but laugh. Getting to the top of the mountain and beating the run feels satisfying, rewarding, and so so so deserved.

While PEAK is obviously best played with friends. Despite that, the exploration, resource management, and constant decision making are satisfying enough on their own to make just a really solid roguelike, even while playing solo. 

Also it has pretty neat lore hidden, which you can find if you pay enough attention. It's pretty cool.

Anyway all this to say, there's a reason the friendslop genre hasn't really gotten much bigger than this game. This game is truly and utterly, PEAK

The physics-based movement creates plenty of funny moments, but beneath the chaos is a surprisingly satisfying survival and teamwork experience. Communication matters, mistakes have consequences, and reaching a new checkpoint feels like a genuine achievement.

If you enjoy co-op games that test teamwork, patience, and friendship, PEAK is absolutely worth the climb.

review:
PEAK is a physics based adventure game, where you alone or with others suffer a plane crash and wake up on a mysterious island. In order to get away from the island you need to climb to the peak which you can reach by going through the island's different regions, surviving the nature and the climb.

The graphics looks cartoonish, but fits perfectly with the game's style. It's colorful and sometimes detailed enough, but only for those things which needs the extra details. Also, the characters and the customization is alright, you can change 6-7 different things on your character, additionally you can unlock some new things which you can acquire to your own avatar.
Controls may seem difficult at first, but after some time the player easily can get into it.
Soundtrack is okay, usually there are not many music tracks to listen to as the game's ambient takes the leading role, however any other sound effects and especially the in game voice chat is really well done. Especially the voice chat, which can change the voice of the other players depending on their location, if they are moving or what place they talk at, like if they are in a cave there is reverb in the voice and so on, which is pretty cool and can make some fun moments.

Finally, one of the best thing in this game is the gameplay. Even though this is just a climbing game there are many game mechanics, items, regions and a few secrets which the player going to explore and figuring these things out, and that is so much fun in PEAK. I could details what things I like in here, but I really do believe it's best to explore this game without "spoiling" some of these things.
Even figuring out how to play game: there is no tutorial for PEAK, however the very first region, which is the Shore, is constructed in such way that the player can check and try the fundamentals which gives a directionless tutorial mode basically, and with this you can enjoy the game in your own pace and won't be slowed down by the game itself. It can be considered as a trial-error type of gameplay, but I believe this is how PEAK needs to be experienced. Once you figure these out then you start thinking about how to optimize your climbing, which is not that straightforward as you may think and to me that's also pretty cool thing to do. Not even mentioning when you can play with your friends, which make the game such a chaotic fun in some cases, or it can feel good when the group works together and reach the top of the island. You can also play it alone, which also works, but in the long term this game works best with others.
Also, every day the island is going changing, so even if you played through the game once you can play a new map with new regions and generations again, which can give additional challenges. Even if you see a region which you already overcome, the regions have different types in itself and also the generations can make different map basically, so there is more than enough replay value in this game. Also also, you can unlock additional difficulty levels which can give extra challenges in future run.
I also want to mention the in-game accolades, which are basically the achievements for PEAK. In my reviews I really don't highlight achievements for a game, because I like to play it in my own pace and do what things in the game which I feel like to do, but in PEAK these accolades unlock new character customization items if you complete them, but also they give incentives to try out new things in a run, which is also interesting to explore.

There are many positives things about PEAK, but there are a few negative things too. There were a couple of times when I got disconnected from an online match, due to timeout... which is weird, because I did not lose internet connection and this happened randomly, and to others in my lobby. You can invite players mid run, but this can be annoying to get into, as it comes up out of nowhere.
One thing which is good to know, is PEAK is a 4 player game. If you have more people to play with, the vanilla game don't have the option to play with more sadly, however there is a mod which can delete this limitation and play with more people.
Also, occasionally there are some weird generations which can make the game more broken, like when two objects is generated in each other or when certain items are in one location. So far I did not encounter anything game breaking, and also as far as I know the devs checks the maps beforehand, but this is something which is good to keep in mind.
And I hope there will be more regions to explore or new things to find in existing regions, because even though the regions have different generation types in itself, after a couple of hours they might start to feel flat for some people.

Another thing I'd love to see is the ability to create lobbies larger than four players without the need for mods. I personally love to use mods in general, but since PEAK is also a very family-friendly game and many people don't like using mods, I'd like to see the option to create bigger lobbies without them. All in all, PEAK is an incredibly funny game and I can highly recommend it to anyone who's searching for a quirky alternation with friends and randoms, or an adventurous, almost meditative single-player experience. Not to unmention the various ascents (difficulties). They force you to try different packing methods, adapt your typical climbing tactics, use new paths to reach the peak, and in the end, get another cool cosmetic as reward for each ascent, which also definitely increases the replayability.

[b]No matter if you just wanna reach the Peak a few times with your friends, or go all in for achievement hunting and the full adventure trip, it's worth the price with or without a discount.[/b]

I’m resisting the temptation to make the joke about how “PEAK is Peak”.
PEAK is a climbing game, it’s best experienced cooperative with friends, however you can play by yourself too… but with voice proximity chat, extra hands, extra inventory space, sharing the load, huddling together for warmth, pulling up a friend that extra couple of inches when their stamina runs out, PEAK really is more geared towards a cooperative experience where you summate the mountain together.

[u][b]-Detailed breakdown review-[/b][/u]
[b]Story:[/b] You are a scout… I mean obviously you are a scout, but I mean in the game you play as a Scout. Kinda like “Boy Scouts”, “Girl Scouts”, “Junior Woodchucks”, or “Junior Chipmunk”, go on hikes, learn how to tie square knots, camping, sit in a classroom and do underwater basket weaving… if that last example seems odd, it’s because my time in boy scouts wasn’t stellar.
Anyway, you’re all on a troop adventure and… …Oops! Looks like the plane crashed and only you and your friends survived. It’s up to You and maybe Huey, Dewey or Lewy (friends sold separately) to make it to the PEAK where some idiot lost all of the flares to summon the helicopter to escape. But to get to the Peak… ahh, that’s where the story truly is.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3532803580

[b]Gameplay:[/b] For a game about hiking… There's a fair bit to explain about the gameplay.
First thing you should know is if you want to climb something you walk to a tree, rock, wall or something, click and hold the left mouse button to climb. General movement is with WASD, and when you’re climbing WASD translates to the wall the same way, W is up, S is down, D is right, and A is left. 
After movement is figured out, the next concept which is CRITIALLY important to master is Stamina. It’s definitely a case of “Easy to Learn, Hard to Master”, at the bottom left of the screen you have a stamina bar, once this bar empties you stop climbing and start falling, if the gods of PEAK really hate you, the mountain will slope away and you’ll just fall thousands of feet to unceremoniously hit the floor and bounce once before you drift into unconsciousness.
So you want as much stamina as possible, right? Right! But it’s more complicated then that. Things eat away at your stamina bar, like poison, injuries, burning, freezing, weight from items in your pockets or backpack, and hunger too literally takes chunks out of your stamina bar.

Some food items, or cooked food, or Campfire checkouts will give you bits of a second stamina bar. This second stamina bar is “Bonus Stamina”, if you use up your normal stamina you’ll dip into these reserves which are quite literally CLUTCH. That being said, try not to use bonus stamina unless you need too, everything on peak becomes an exercise in weighing the risks vs rewards…
Do you want to use your bonus stamina to clear this part, and then drop a role for your friends? Or do you want to use a rope cannon and save your bonus stamina? Maybe you don’t have much to work with at all and you should try looking up another side of the mountain… for a potentially easier path? At the end of the day that’s where the real challenge in PEAK is, it’s planning and using your tools effectively and efficiently.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3560585795

[b]Conclusion:[/b] PEAK is really fun! The MESA update was… frustrating. Sometimes you’ll get a generated seed which is just god-awful, and you get to quit the game sad on that day… but you can know tomorrow there’ll be a new generated seed to try out and maybe that one will be easier?
On the whole PEAK has been a fun game, I look forward to any future updates the game might have. I can easily suggest the game for anyone looking for a cooperative game to play with friends. PEAK is very unique, I haven’t played any other game like it, and it’ll sit in my list of “favorite co-op games” probably for the rest of my life.

Now, three hours later, I am dangling by a single pixel off a sheer cliff face. My entire life depends on my buddy, who is currently hyperventilating into his mic because his hand is slipping on his desk. "HOLD ME," I’m screeching, watching the literal lava at the bottom of image_69df55.png mock our existence. One tiny, microscopic slip of the mouse—one minor physics jank—and we are both plummeting 40 minutes of vertical progress straight back to the lobby.

I haven't blinked in ten minutes. My hand is actively cramping from gripping my mouse like my actual life depends on it. I came here for a "co-op physics adventure," but my heart rate is higher than it’s ever been in my life. Mixed Feelings – Fun concept, frustrating direction

PEAK is, at its core, a co-op game meant for laughs, teamwork, and the shared struggle of the climb. When it’s working, it’s a blast — the silly moments, the coordination, and the feeling of slowly overcoming obstacles together are genuinely enjoyable.

Most people play PEAK for the goofy co-op experience and a sense of progression with some challenge, not to be endlessly punished by near-impossible climbs. Right now, many players struggle to complete even a single run after several hours, and yet updates seem to focus on making things even harder.

I hope future updates focus more on keeping the experience enjoyable and achievable, rather than just increasing the difficulty curve.

[i]PEAK[/i] is a mountaineering, survival platformer. Balancing resources, helping one another in co-op, and taking risks to ascend up towards your goal is all part of the fun. There is a lot of artistry and effort put into this wonderful game with its straightforward objective to reach the top. While the game is designed with multiplayer in mind, it is also incredibly good even when trekking it alone.

The game is well crafted visually in its daily random map generation and character designs. Biomes have distinct aesthetics which come with their own unique set of hazards. They challenge players with different kinds of environmental obstacles -- including various fauna -- and weather conditions. The terrain for each biome never look out of place due to the excellent use of shadows and lighting, and objects and flora are seamlessly integrated into the environment. In addition, the sound design really lends itself to the tone and atmosphere of each biome in its ambience. The music, or lack thereof at times, also emphasizes the feelings of isolation (especially in solo expeditions) or the pressure to continually move upwards and onwards or face dire consequences. A lot of care was also put into characters as well with player characters having charming and expressive designs. Their colorful, cartoony look makes players easy to spot from the environment. The effort put into making visible responses for various player actions and gameplay movements make things feel more natural in co-op sessions. Mouths that move while using proximity chat and eyes that follow you when you're close are nice touches. The addition of emotes and the ability to point things out for everyone are appreciated.

As a survival platformer, the game can be unforgiving. You and your group's pathfinding skills will be put to the test as you ascend towards the peak. Whether going in alone with no others to rely on or as part of a group of friends (and setting aside any hijinks between players), balancing cautiousness and speed will be essential and you must use items and tools as efficiently as possible and take risks when necessary in order to proceed. The goal of reaching the summit can be a puzzle all on its own while minimizing injuries but there are also various ways how each biome can throw debuffs at you with its challenges such as hunger or poison. They will impede a player's stamina which makes climbing more difficult. In later difficulties the game not only makes climbing harder to do, but it also adds pressure on players with a long-term doom counter that forces players to race against time as well or die. Yes, dying sucks but the variety and ways players can overcome challenges keeps things interesting. In a group it's best to work together, share resources, and help each other by literally lending a helping hand to pull friends up. But if someone does die and have not yet been revived, then it's not the end for them. Dead players will return as ghosts to haunt your friends. Though ideally they'll help their living counterparts by pointing out the best routes or items. (Who packs a [i]cannon[/i] in their luggage anyway? On a side note though, I love how the game incorporates the tutorial by way of minigames and the player lobby seamlessly into the game's world. I also love how Steam achievements are directly tied to the badges on a player character's sash.) Thankfully, the game eases players into the world of [i]PEAK[/i] with smaller challenges before the bigger, do-or-die challenges found later. Players always start on the "Shore" after waking from the plane crash to get them rolling. Reaching the end of a biome allows players to recuperate a bit and revive any dead party members before pressing on until the players ultimately reach "The Kiln", the final area before the peak, which requires players to use all their honed skills and items to overcome.

[i]PEAK[/i] is an excellently designed game for both single player and multiplayer. The game makes players think about their pathfinding and how to use any found tools in the best possible way. The game can be difficult and can sometimes be frustrating, but when you or your group finally reach the peak there's always a sense of relief and joy. And always remember "Rule 0", my friends, [b]never abandon a friend in need.[/b]

TL;DR: Fun and colourful but sometimes frustrating coop game about climbing and finding your way through worlds that change daily. This review is written from a "pre-finished" viewpoint (at the time of this review, I haven't played through the whole game).

From Team PEAK and the publishers Aggro Crab and Landfall comes PEAK, a coop climbing/find your way game for up to four simulatenous players.

The premise of the game is that you and your fellow players board a plane and tragedy strikes. The plane crashes and you're stranded on some unknown island. Suddenly, you're fighting for your survival and trying to reach civilization once again.
Not only do you have to scale difficult terrain, you also have to find some food to keep going. The better you're fed, the more stamina you have to tackle your challenges. And on top of that - at least with the Roots update - you will also encounter enemy-type creatures that are out to get you. And then there's some additional "natural" obstacles and conditions like heavy wind which will hinder your progress, so you'll have to learn how to deal with that. Also... you can slip on some objects, so watch your step!

You have to get to know your surroundings, learn which plants might be safe to eat or which herb does help in certain situations. There's some help if you keep your eyes peeled: you can find some written tips to help you understand what's what. You can also find items that may help you on your way through the game - or some that might just be cluttering your inventory, depending on your playstyle. Think of ropes you can use to help your fellow players reach areas they might not be able to climb anymore because they are hurt or out of stamina. Or think of noisy little trumpets you can use to annoy your friends. "Ah, there's an inventory?" you might ask. Yes. But it is limited to three slots plus a backpack. And you have to search for those backpacks, since they're not too easy to come by.

The graphics are colourful, the player characters being depicted in a cartoonish style with some customisation options like diverse facial expressions or different clothing (some of which needs to be unlocked by playing the game). The areas you reach are kind of themed, starting you in a rocky beach area and encountering others like a huge mushroom forest (this came in with the roots update) or lava areas - among others. Each "biome" has its own difficulties and quirks you have to
manage.

I have to say the music seems relaxing most of the time and since the situations can get a bit tense that's very welcome. As I use to say: if the sounds don't feel out of place for you, they did a good job. And as of now I don't feel that the sound effects are misplaced at all. Also I didn't notice any "too loud/too silent"-type problems. Aaaaaand of course the game has microphone capabilities, so... just mute your discord if you want to use the in-game voice chat options. This is fun because sometimes you get lost or separated and can listen for the voices of your fellow players in the distance. Or listen to their screams when they plummet to their deaths.
Yes, there is a "death mechanic". Players who suffered heavy injuries will KO and be able to follow the other still alive players around and talk to them, so you're not completely out of the game. If your friends reach certain areas you can get revived and continue the stressful journey.

Earlier I wrote that the game can get "frustrating". Yeah, I've stood in front of some walls/mountains and asked myself: "How? How in the hell should this be possible?". And I'm not sure if every scenario is "doable", but that's kind of the design I guess.
You will fall. You will reach dead ends. There will be environmental hazards that will neutralize you at the worst timing possible. If you can live with that, you're fine.

At the time of this review, the devs still care for the game, putting out bug fixes and additions to the game. We all like that, don't we? For you achievement hunters: currently there are 54 steam achievements you can work towards and none of those seem too over the top, although a lot of them are circumstancial.

The friends I'm playing with and me still have to finish the game, so I don't know everything yet. There's still a lot for us to find out about the game so I guess this review isn't too "spoilery".

Thanks for reading,
Ossel

With stamina dwindling, hazards lurking, and the environment shifting daily, you and your fellow scouts must climb, slip, fall, laugh, and improvise your way toward the Peak.

[b] Overall [/b]
PEAK is charming and chaotic. The physics-driven climbing feels tactile and fun, especially when paired with friends who can rescue or sabotage you and daily rotating mountain layout help keep the game experience fresh. Though the survival mechanics are intentionally light and solo play can feel tougher, the game delivers a memorable co-op journey packed with emergent moments and shared laughter. For its price, PEAK is absolutely worth it.
